provenance.other: “transparent glass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 21:21. The nearest neighbours are “clear as crystal”, which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 4:6 and 22:1 — both also of the heavenly city.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed phrase turns out to describe a city that needs no lamp: “the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it” (Revelation 21:23). Ether 3 is about exactly that — a light source that is not a fire, made by God touching stone. The brother of Jared is asking for, and gets, a fragment of the New Jerusalem's optics four verses before he is shown the Lord who lights it.

3:1.note: The sixteen stones are “white and clear, even as transparent glass”. The comparison is the KJV's, and the KJV uses it once: the street of the New Jerusalem, “pure gold, as it were transparent glass”. Nothing else in the King James Bible is transparent. Two considerations keep this at moderate rather than high — “glass” is a natural word for anyone describing molten silica, and the shared string is two words, well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and below what §2 would want for an allusion. But the writer had a choice of comparisons for a clear stone (crystal, ice, water, the sapphire pavement of Exodus 24:10) and reached for the one the KJV uses of the city of light.
3:1.text: And the twelve gates were twelve pearls: every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

provenance.other: “the top of the mount” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; three of them (Exodus 19:20, 24:17, 34:2) are Sinai, one is Aaron's death on Hor, one is David on Olivet. “tables of stone” occurs in exactly thirteen KJV verses, every one of them Sinai or its recital.
provenance.significance: The chapter's whole shape is Exodus 34 with the tablets replaced by lamps. Moses hews stone out of the mountain, carries it in his hand to the top of the mount, and God writes on it with his finger; the brother of Jared moultens stone out of a rock, carries it in his hands to the top of the mount, and God touches it with his finger. What Sinai's stones carry away is a law; what Shelem's carry away is light. The catalogue reads the substitution as the point, not as a coincidence of props — and Ether 3:23's “these two stones will I give unto thee” closes the frame on Exodus 24:12's “I will give thee tables of stone”.

3:1.note: “Went forth unto the mount … because of its exceeding height, and did moulten out of a rock sixteen small stones … and he did carry them in his hands upon the top of the mount.” There is no long verbal run here and the argument does not need one: the sequence is Exodus 34:4's, element for element and in order — stone worked out of rock by a man, carried in the hand, taken up a named mountain, presented to God, marked by God's own finger (Ether 3:4, 3:6; Exodus 31:18). The Book of Mormon has already been quarrying this stretch of the Pentateuch in this book — Ether 2:4-5 runs on Numbers 11:25 and Deuteronomy 1:33 — so the recurrence criterion is doing real work. Note that where Moses carries two tables the brother of Jared carries sixteen stones, and where Moses is summoned the brother of Jared comes uninvited.
3:1.text: And he hewed two tables of stone like unto the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up unto mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand the two tables of stone.

provenance.other: “evil continually” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:5. The book of Ether has Genesis 6-8 open throughout: Ether 2:15 quotes Genesis 6:3, 2:17 follows Genesis 7:16, 2:23 follows Genesis 6:16, and 3:15 will reach Genesis 6:7.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is unusually exact. Genesis 6:5 is the verdict that causes the flood — God sees that man's heart is “only evil continually” and resolves to drown the earth. The brother of Jared pronounces that verdict on himself in the same two words, in a prayer whose opening clause is “thou hast said that we must be encompassed about by the floods”. He confesses the reason for the deluge while asking to be carried through one. In Genesis the sentence destroys; in Ether the man who accepts the sentence is preserved in a sealed vessel, which is what Noah was.

3:2.note: “Because of the fall, our natures have become evil continually.” Two words, and they are the King James Bible's two words for the state of the antediluvian heart, in a book whose barges are built out of Genesis 6:16 and whose commission is dated by Genesis 6:3. The 1830 and 1920 texts agree here, so nothing hangs on the edition; what hangs on the phrase is that Ether 3's petitioner opens by placing himself, verbally, inside the flood narrative he is about to re-enact.
3:2.text: And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.

provenance.other: “dwellest in the heavens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 123:1. The near variants are Psalm 2:4 (“He that sitteth in the heavens”) and Isaiah 57:15 (“I dwell in the high and holy place”), neither of which is second person.
provenance.significance: Psalm 123 is the shortest of the Songs of Degrees and its whole burden is a servant's eye fixed on a master's hand until mercy comes — “as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters”. Ether 3:2-6 is a servant asking that a hand be stretched out, and getting it. The psalm supplies the posture the chapter then dramatises.

3:2.note: “We know that thou art holy, and dwellest in the heavens, and that we are unworthy before thee.” The second-person address to the one who dwells in the heavens is a KJV singleton, and the verse it comes from is a plea from an unworthy servant to a master's hand. Held at moderate because a writer composing a prayer of unworthiness could arrive at the phrase without Psalm 123 in front of him; recorded because the psalm's controlling image is the hand, which is what this prayer is about to ask for.
3:2.text: Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens.

provenance.other: “Oh let not the LORD be angry” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 18:30 and 18:32, both in Abraham's bargaining at Mamre. There is no other KJV formula for a man apologising in advance for pressing God further.
provenance.significance: Abraham's phrase is the Bible's licence for importunity: it is said twice, each time as the prelude to asking for more than was asked for last time, and each time God concedes. Ether 3 is the Book of Mormon's great scene of importunity — a man who asks for light, then asks to be shown the Lord, then is not refused — and it opens with Abraham's disclaimer.

3:2.note: “Do not be angry with thy servant because of his weakness before thee.” The wording is not the KJV's word for word, which is why this is moderate rather than high, but the speech act is Genesis 18:30's and the KJV has only one place for it. Note what the two contexts share beyond the formula: in Genesis the deferential clause precedes an escalating request, and here it precedes the escalation from stones to a face. Note too what has been substituted — Abraham excuses himself as “dust and ashes”, the brother of Jared as weak, which is the term Ether 12:27 will make the book's own.
3:2.text: And he said unto him, Oh let not the LORD be angry, and I will speak: Peradventure there shall thirty be found there. And he said, I will not do it, if I find thirty there.

provenance.other: “turn from thy fierce wrath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 32:12. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, “turn away thine anger”, is in no KJV verse at all, which is why kjvSpecific is held at uncertain rather than raised to yes.
provenance.significance: The one place in the King James Bible where a man on a mountain asks God to turn away wrath from “thy people” is Moses' intercession after the golden calf — and Moses is at that moment holding, or about to hold, the two tables of stone. Ether 3 puts its intercessor on a mountain with stones in his hands and gives him the same request. The Sinai frame opened at 3:1 is being kept, and kept at the point where Sinai's stones are broken.

3:3.note: “Turn away thine anger from this thy people, and suffer not that they shall go forth across this raging deep in darkness.” The phrasing is not the KJV's, and the honest reading of the evidence is that the dependence is at the level of the scene rather than the sentence. What makes it worth cataloguing is the coincidence of role: a mediator on a mountain, stones in hand, asking God to turn from anger against a people who are described as his rather than the speaker's — that is Exodus 32:11-12 and, in the KJV, essentially nowhere else. Compare Hays on thematic coherence: the criterion doing the work here is context, not volume.
3:3.text: Wherefore should the Egyptians speak, and say, For mischief did he bring them out, to slay them in the mountains, and to consume them from the face of the earth? Turn from thy fierce wrath, and repent of this evil against thy people.

provenance.other: “I know, O LORD, that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 119:75; Job 42:2 supplies the same opening without the vocative (“I know that thou canst do every thing”) and adds the clause about withholding. “canst do every thing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 42:2.
provenance.significance: The strongest evidence for Job here is not in 3:4 but in 3:26, where the chapter returns to the second half of the same verse: Job 42:2 pairs “thou canst do every thing” with “no thought can be withholden from thee”, and Ether 3:26 pairs “the Lord could shew him all things” with “the Lord could not withhold any thing from him”. Both halves of one short KJV verse, twenty-two verses apart, in the same order. And Job 42:5 — “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee” — is the exact movement of Ether 3 from report to sight, which 3:19 states as doctrine when it says the man “had faith no longer, for he knew”.

3:4.note: “And I know, O Lord, that thou hast all power, and can do whatsoever thou wilt.” Job 42:2 is the KJV's one sentence in which a man tells God he can do everything, and the Book of Mormon has it with Psalm 119:75's vocative slotted in. The rarity is doing real work — “canst do every thing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — but the case rests on the pair: this verse takes Job's first clause and 3:26 takes his second, and Job 42:2's second clause is about withholding, which is a strange thing for a chapter about lamps to circle back to unless it came from there.
3:4.text: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.

provenance.other: “finger of God” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Exodus 8:19 (the magicians' confession), Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10 (the tables written at Sinai), and Luke 11:20 (“if I with the finger of God cast out devils”). Only Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10 bring the finger and worked stone into one sentence.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible God's finger does three things: it writes on stone, it works a plague Egypt's magicians cannot match, and — in Luke's mouth — it casts out devils as the sign that the kingdom has come. Ether 3:4 asks it to do a fourth thing, and asks on the strength of the first: the petition names stones, the finger, and a mountain in one breath, which is Exodus 31:18's inventory exactly. The metaleptic payoff arrives two verses later, when the finger that in Exodus writes invisibly on the far side of a cloud is seen, and turns out to belong to a body.

3:4.note: “Therefore touch these stones, O Lord, with thy finger, and prepare them that they may shine forth in darkness.” The request is unprecedented; the vocabulary is not. “Finger of God” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and two of them are the Sinai tablets, where the finger's one recorded action on stone is inscription. The brother of Jared asks for the same gesture and a different result, and the chapter then presses the borrowed image further than any of its sources do: Exodus never says what the finger looked like, and Ether 3:6 does.
3:4.text: And he gave unto Moses, when he had made an end of communing with him upon mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God.

provenance.other: “the foolishness of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:25. There is no shared string with Ether 3:5, which is why kjvSpecific is 'no'.
provenance.significance: Ether is the book that ends by quoting 2 Corinthians 12:9 outright — “my grace is sufficient”, at Ether 12:27, with weakness made strong — and 1 Corinthians 1:25 is the other half of Paul's paradox, divine power that looks like its opposite to human judgment. Reading 3:5 with 12:26-27 makes the brother of Jared's sentence the premise of Moroni's later argument rather than a stray piece of piety: what looks small to the understanding of men is where God works, which is precisely why sixteen pebbles are the vehicle of the revelation.

3:5.note: “We know that thou art able to shew forth great power, which looks small unto the understanding of men.” There is no verbal contact, and the entry is filed on thematic coherence alone: the sentence states Paul's paradox of 1 Corinthians 1:25 in its own words, in a book that will quote the companion paradox of 2 Corinthians 12:9 almost verbatim at 12:27. Recorded at moderate because the coincidence of doctrine with a book that demonstrably has Paul's weakness-language to hand is worth more than the wording alone would justify, and less than a verbal case would.
3:5.text: Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

provenance.other: “the vail shall be taken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:16. Note the KJV's two spellings, which matter for this chapter: the tabernacle passages read “vail” and Hebrews 6:19 reads “veil”, and Ether 3:19-20 follows Hebrews.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most consequential borrowing and the least noticed. 2 Corinthians 3 is an argument about Moses' veil — the covering Moses put on his face coming down from the mount (Exodus 34:33-35), which Paul turns into a figure for a covering on the mind that is removed by turning to the Lord. Ether 3 has been running the Sinai ascent since 3:1; at the moment of contact the veil that lifts is not Moses' cloth but Paul's, and it lifts from the eyes rather than the face. The unstated correspondence is the whole of Paul's point: “when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away”, and what the brother of Jared then sees is the Lord.

3:6.note: “The veil was taken from off the eyes of the brother of Jared, and he saw the finger of the Lord.” The passive construction is 2 Corinthians 3:16's and the KJV has it once. Two things raise this above a coincidence of a common noun. First, the surrounding chapter has been building a Sinai ascent, and 2 Corinthians 3 is the New Testament's one sustained reading of what happened to Moses' face on that ascent. Second, the same veil returns twice more in a technical sense at 3:19-20 (“within the veil”) and again at Ether 12:19, so the image is load-bearing across the book and not a single flourish.
3:6.text: Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away.

provenance.other: “fingers of a man's hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 5:5. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, the finger of a man, appears in no KJV verse; Daniel 5:5 is the only place in the King James Bible where a disembodied divine hand is described as a man's.
provenance.significance: Recover Daniel 5 and the chapter's second half is already there. What the man's fingers do at Belshazzar's feast is write a text nobody present can read, which a seer must be fetched to interpret; sixteen verses after Ether 3:6 the Lord tells the brother of Jared to write in “a language that they cannot be read” and gives him two stones so that in due time the writing “shall magnify to the eyes of men”. Daniel supplies the one KJV image that holds a visible divine finger and an unreadable divinely-given script together, and Ether 3 uses both halves.

3:6.note: “He saw the finger of the Lord; and it was as the finger of a man, like unto flesh and blood.” The King James Bible describes a divine finger as a man's exactly once, at Belshazzar's wall. The contact is three words and is held at moderate for that reason — a writer needing to say that a finger looked human has few other ways to say it. What lifts it above chance is the second coincidence: the Daniel scene is about writing that cannot be read without a gift of interpretation, which is what the same chapter's closing commission (3:22-24) is about, and the catalogue treats the pairing as evidence rather than the phrase alone.
3:6.text: In the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king’s palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote.

provenance.other: “wherefore liest thou” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 7:10. It is the only place in the King James Bible where God answers a prostrate man with an imperative to rise followed by an interrogative reproach; Daniel 10:11's “stand upright” is the nearest neighbour and has no question.
provenance.significance: The suppressed half of the correspondence is why Joshua is on his face: Israel has just been beaten at Ai because Achan has stolen from the accursed thing, and God's “wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?” means stop praying and go find the sin. Ether 3:7 uses the identical construction with the identical words in the identical situation and means the exact opposite — there is no sin, and the question is astonishment. The catalogue reads the reversal as the finding. The formula that in Joshua interrupts an intercession because it is misplaced here interrupts a prostration because it is unnecessary.

3:7.note: “And the Lord said unto him, Arise, why hast thou fallen?” Two clauses, and both are Joshua 7:10's: “Get thee up” and “wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?” The King James Bible has one other verse in this neighbourhood, Daniel 10:11, and it lacks the question. The 1830 text reads “why hast thou fallen”, which is the sense of the KJV's “liest thou” in plainer English rather than a distinct idiom. Below Skousen's threshold and well below a quotation, but the syntactic shape — vocative imperative, then an interrogative about the posture — is a King James pattern with a single instance.
3:7.text: And the LORD said unto Joshua, Get thee up; wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?

provenance.other: The machine stream ranked Judges 6:21 on the four-word run “his hand and touched the”; the argument here is for the three verses together, of which only 6:21 shares wording.
provenance.significance: Judges 6:21-23 is the King James Bible's compact type-scene for this exact moment: an angel puts out a hand and touches, the man perceives who it was, and the man's first words are that he has seen God and expects to die — to which the answer is “fear not: thou shalt not die.” Ether 3:6-9 runs the same four beats: hand stretched forth and touching, perception, “I feared lest he should smite me”, and a reassurance that turns into a revelation. What Ether adds is the reason the fear was misplaced, and it is a Christological one: not merely that God spares, but that the hand was always going to be flesh.

3:8.note: “I saw the finger of the Lord, and I feared lest he should smite me: for I knew not that the Lord had flesh and blood.” The dread of dying because one has seen a divine being is a fixed KJV reaction, and its fullest statement is Gideon's: “Alas, O LORD God! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face” — a sentence that follows, two verses earlier, an angel putting forth his hand and touching. The verbal contact is thin and the sequence is not: touch, recognition, fear of death, reassurance, in that order in both. Filed at high on sequence and context rather than on volume, and kjvSpecific left uncertain because the shared wording will not carry a claim about English versions.
3:8.text: And when Gideon perceived that he was an angel of the LORD, Gideon said, Alas, O LORD God! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face.

provenance.other: “I knew not that” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Numbers 22:34 and Jeremiah 11:19; only the first is a confession to a divine being. “fell flat on his face” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 22:31.
provenance.significance: The Balaam scene supplies the whole three-verse movement of Ether 3:6-8, and supplies it in the same order: “the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD … and he bowed down his head, and fell flat on his face”, then “I have sinned; for I knew not that thou stoodest in the way.” Ether 3:6-8 has the veil taken from off the eyes, the seeing, the falling down, and “I knew not that the Lord had flesh and blood”. And the chapter goes back to Balaam four verses later: the confession at 3:12 that God “canst not lie” is, in the King James Bible, most nearly Numbers 23:19 — “God is not a man, that he should lie” — said to a man who has just been told that God will become one.

3:8.note: “For I knew not that the Lord had flesh and blood.” The formula of a man excusing his failure to recognise a divine presence is Numbers 22:34's, and the KJV has it in only one other verse, where the speaker is Jeremiah and the ignorance is of a human plot. Held at moderate because “I knew not that” is short and unremarkable in itself; recorded because it sits at the end of a three-step sequence — eyes opened, seeing, falling — that Numbers 22:31 supplies entire, and because the same Balaam oracle returns at 3:12.
3:8.text: And Balaam said unto the angel of the LORD, I have sinned; for I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me: now therefore, if it displease thee, I will get me back again.

provenance.other: “flesh and blood” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Matthew 16:17, 1 Corinthians 15:50, Galatians 1:16, Ephesians 6:12, Hebrews 2:14 — and every one of them is in the New Testament. “partakers of flesh and blood” and “took part of the same” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, both Hebrews 2:14.
provenance.significance: The availability problem is at its sharpest here and, per CONVENTIONS §3a, that is the finding rather than an objection. The phrase in which the Lord announces his incarnation to a man living before Abraham exists nowhere in the Old Testament: all five King James occurrences of “flesh and blood” are New Testament, and the only one that means the incarnation is Hebrews 2:14, where the Son takes part in flesh and blood in order to destroy death through death. Ether 3:9's “I shall take upon me flesh and blood” is that sentence in the first person and the future tense — the epistle's argument spoken by its subject, before the fact.

3:9.note: “Because of thy faith thou hast seen that I shall take upon me flesh and blood.” The idiom is exclusively a New Testament one in the King James Bible, and Hebrews 2:14 is the single verse where it carries the doctrine Ether 3 is stating: that the Son took what the children are partakers of. The chapter uses the phrase twice, at 3:8 and 3:9, once for what the brother of Jared did not know and once for what he is now told, and both times in the vocabulary of a first-century Greek epistle. Below a quotation on length and above an echo on distinctiveness; the borrowing is of a doctrinal formula, not a clause.
3:9.text: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;

provenance.other: “blessed are they that have not seen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:29. The catalogue already carries John 20:27 as a certain link at 3 Nephi 11:14, where the risen Christ invites the Nephites to thrust their hands into his side — so the Thomas pericope is demonstrably available to the writer of this book and is used elsewhere in it.
provenance.significance: Ether 3:9 is John 20:29 turned around, clause for clause. Jesus tells Thomas “because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed”; the Lord tells the brother of Jared “because of thy faith thou hast seen”. Sight produces belief in John and belief produces sight in Ether, and the reversal is the doctrine the chapter exists to state — completed at 3:19, where the man “had faith no longer, for he knew”, which is the exact position John 20:29 calls less blessed. Whether the inversion is a correction of John or a compliment to him is the question the entry leaves open; that it is an inversion of John and not an independent formulation is what the wording shows.

3:9.note: “Because of thy faith thou hast seen … for were it so, ye could not have seen my finger.” The Fourth Gospel's closing beatitude is the one place in the King James Bible where seeing and believing are set in a causal order and ranked, and Ether 3:9 states the reverse order as a law. Note that the finger is Thomas's word too: “except I shall … put my finger into the print of the nails, I will not believe” (John 20:25). A chapter in which a man is shown a finger and told that faith is what let him see it is running on John 20 whether or not it names it, and this book uses that pericope again at 3 Nephi 11:14.
3:9.text: Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

provenance.other: “so great faith” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and its Lukan parallel at 7:9. Both are the same saying, and it is the only superlative Christ pronounces about anyone's faith in the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: The suppressed half is the words that follow: “I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.” The one time the King James Christ ranks a man's faith above all comers, the man is a Gentile centurion and the point of the sentence is that Israel has been outdone from outside. Ether 3:9 makes the same pronouncement over a man who is not merely a Gentile but pre-Israelite — the covenant does not yet exist, Abraham has not been called, and the superlative is therefore not even a comparison Israel could lose. Read alongside Matthew 8:10, the verse is an argument about where faith is found.

3:9.note: “Never has man come before me with such exceeding faith as thou hast.” The verbal contact is a superlative and the word faith, which is why this is an echo at moderate and not more. It is recorded because the King James Bible contains exactly one such pronouncement from Christ's mouth, at Matthew 8:10 and its Lukan twin, and because the pronouncement is made there about an outsider — the same structural point Ether 3 makes by putting its theophany in Mesopotamia at the dispersion instead of in Israel.
3:9.text: When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

provenance.other: “Believest thou” as a bare interrogative occurs in exactly four KJV verses — John 1:50, 11:26, 14:10 and Acts 26:27 — of which three are Johannine. Only John 1:50 answers its own question with a promise of greater sight.
provenance.significance: John 1:50-51 is the pattern of Ether 3:11-13 in miniature: a question testing belief, an affirmative, and then “thou shalt see greater things than these … ye shall see heaven open”. The chapter has already drawn on John 1 twice by 3:14 (the light in darkness of 1:5, the power to become sons of 1:12) and will draw on it again at 3:16 and 3:15. Nathanael's exchange is where the prologue's Christology first becomes a scene, and Ether 3 is the Book of Mormon's scene of the same shape.

3:11.note: “Believest thou the words which I shall speak? … And when he had said these words, behold, the Lord shewed himself unto him.” The interrogative is a Johannine formula with four King James instances, and the one that matters is John 1:50, where the question is followed immediately by an escalation of vision. The structural agreement is exact — belief tested before sight is granted, and the sight granted exceeds the sight already had — and it sits inside a chapter that reaches John 1 at four separate points. Filed at high on sequence and recurrence rather than on the two shared words.
3:11.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 32:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the second clause from Titus 1:2
provenance.other: “a God of truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 32:4. “cannot lie” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Titus 1:2. Ether 3:12 has both in a single sentence, which no KJV verse does.
provenance.significance: The chapter fuses the Song of Moses with the Pastoral Epistles and the seam is where the interest lies. Deuteronomy 32:4 opens “He is the Rock” — the verse the brother of Jared quotes is a verse about God as rock, said by a man who has spent the chapter moultening stones out of one. And the nearest King James statement of the doctrine he is confessing is not Titus but Numbers 23:19, “God is not a man, that he should lie” — spoken by Balaam, whose scene the chapter borrowed at 3:8, and flatly contradicted, in its literal sense, by what God is about to say at 3:14-16. The man affirms that God cannot lie one verse before God tells him he will be a man.

3:12.note: “Thou art a God of truth, and canst not lie.” Two clauses, two King James singletons, from opposite ends of the canon: “a God of truth” is Deuteronomy 32:4's alone, “cannot lie” is Titus 1:2's alone, and no King James verse holds them together. The fusion is what makes the entry; a writer with either verse would produce half of this sentence. Deuteronomy is filed as the source and Titus as composite because the Song of Moses is the chapter's register and because its opening words, “He is the Rock”, are the metaphor this chapter has been handling literally since 3:1.
3:12.text: He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.

provenance.route: John 1:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the daughters from 2 Corinthians 6:18
provenance.other: Three separate phrases of John 1:12 are King James singletons and all three occur in that one verse: “believe on his name”, “power to become” and “become the sons of God”. “my sons and my daughters” is also a singleton, but at Genesis 31:28 in Laban's mouth — see the exclusion register at this verse; the daughters come from 2 Corinthians 6:18, “ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty”.
provenance.significance: John 1:12 stands between the prologue's light (1:4-5) and its incarnation (1:14), and Ether 3:14 stands in the same place in its own chapter — between stones that give light and a body that will be flesh. The Book of Mormon takes the middle verse of the prologue's argument and uses it for the middle move of its own, then supplies from 2 Corinthians the daughters that John 1:12 does not have. Recovering John 1 explains what would otherwise be an odd sequence of claims in one verse: pre-existence, light, name, adoption. That is the order of the prologue.

3:14.note: “In me shall all mankind have light … even they which shall believe on my name; and they shall become my sons and my daughters.” Two of the three distinctive elements of John 1:12 are here in John's order — belief on the name, and becoming sons — and each of them is a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 reads “they which shall believe”, with the relative pronoun the KJV uses and the 1920 edition later modernised to “who”, which is a small piece of evidence in the same direction. The daughters are not John's, and 2 Corinthians 6:18 supplies them in the KJV's only formula for the pair as divine speech.
3:14.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: “the light of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:4, and the sentence continues into 1:5's “the light shineth in darkness”; John 8:12 restates the pair as “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness”. Ether 3:14's “In me shall all mankind have light” is the prologue's construction — light located in a person and possessed by others in him — made first-person.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's governing joke, if that is the word — the metaphor is being cashed. The prologue says the light shines in darkness; Ether 3 has a man who needs, quite literally, light that will shine in darkness, and the being who gives it says in the same breath that he is himself the light. Ether 6:3 completes the figure without a trace of metaphor: “thus the Lord caused stones to shine in darkness … that they might not cross the great waters in darkness.” The catalogue's reading is that the chapter is built to make the Johannine sentence a physical fact and then to say it doctrinally in the same verse.

3:14.note: “In me shall all mankind have light, and that eternally.” The construction — light located in a person rather than given by him — is the prologue's and, in the KJV, effectively only the prologue's and its restatement at John 8:12. The evidence here is not volume but position: the sentence stands in a chapter whose plot is a request for light to shine in darkness (3:4), whose fulfilment is described at 6:3 in the prologue's own terms, and which reaches John 1 again at 3:12's neighbour verses and at 3:16. Held at high on coherence and recurrence, with rarity scored low because the individual words are ordinary.
3:14.text: And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

provenance.other: “from the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly six KJV verses; of those, Revelation 13:8 is the only one whose subject is a person rather than a kingdom, a parable or a set of works. “prepared for you from the foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34, which supplies the participle Ether 3:14 uses.
provenance.significance: The composite is the finding. Ether 3:14 needs a redeemer who is a person, who is prepared, and who is so from the foundation of the world; the King James Bible distributes those three across Revelation 13:8 (the Lamb, so slain), Matthew 25:34 (prepared, so dated) and 1 Peter 1:20 (foreordained before the foundation, and afterwards manifest). The third of these is the chapter's own doctrine two verses later — pre-existent now in the spirit, manifest afterward in the flesh — which is why 1 Peter is worth naming even though it reads “before” and not “from”.

3:14.note: “I am he which was prepared from the foundation of the world, to redeem my people.” The dating formula has six King James instances and none of them says quite this; the sentence takes its participle from one (Matthew 25:34) and its referent from another (Revelation 13:8's Lamb slain from the foundation of the world). Filed as an echo at moderate because no single source accounts for the clause and a writer steeped in the phrase could assemble it without any of them — but the assembly is a New Testament one, and the doctrine of a redeemer datable to before the world is not stated in these terms anywhere in the Old Testament.
3:14.text: And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

provenance.other: “created he him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 1:27, and “in the image of God” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 1:27 and 9:6. tools/mediation-check.py was run on this verse against Genesis 1:27, Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6 — the two New Testament citations of the creation of humankind. It reports the Book of Mormon carrying Genesis 1:27's form decisively: both Gospel citations drop “image” altogether and keep only “male and female”, which is the half Ether 3:15 does not use. The route is the Old Testament verse, not its New Testament quotation.
provenance.significance: The verse does two things with Genesis 1 at once. It supplies the doctrinal premise the chapter needs — man is in God's image, therefore God's finger may be a man's — and it dates it, “in the beginning”, which is Genesis 1:1's phrase carried down to 1:27's subject. What the chapter adds is the direction of the likeness: Genesis says man was made in God's image, and Ether 3:16 turns the sentence over to say that the image is a body, and that the body is the one about to be born.

3:15.note: “Seest thou that ye are created after mine own image? Yea, even all men were created, in the beginning, after mine own image.” This is Genesis 1:27 with “in his own image” put in the first person and “in the beginning” fetched from 1:1, and it is stated twice in one verse because the chapter is about to build on it: the whole point of 3:16 is that the image is a body. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 1:27 here and this catalogue reaches it independently; the mediation check settles that the form is the Old Testament's rather than Matthew's or Mark's, which matters because both Gospels cite the passage without the word “image”.
3:15.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

provenance.other: “man whom I have created” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:7.
provenance.alternative: The senses pull apart: in Genesis the clause is the object of “I will destroy”, and here it is the object of a self-revelation withheld. A reader could reasonably say that a five-word run this ordinary in its vocabulary — man, create, the first person — is arithmetic rather than borrowing, and that is why the entry sits at moderate.
provenance.significance: Ether has Genesis 6 open on the desk. The book quotes Genesis 6:3 at 2:15, builds its barges from Genesis 6:16 at 2:23, shuts their door with Genesis 7:16 at 2:17, and takes “evil continually” from Genesis 6:5 at 3:2. On that showing the singleton at 3:15 is more likely to be a fifth draw from the same page than a coincidence — and the draw is pointed: the King James clause for the creature God made and regretted is reused for the creature God has never yet shown himself to, in the same breath as Genesis 1:27's image. Creation, regret, and likeness are being held together.

3:15.note: “Never hath I shewed myself unto man whom I have created.” Five words that occur together in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is the flood sentence. The sense is not the same and the entry does not claim it is; what it claims is that a book which has quarried Genesis 6-7 four times already in twenty-eight verses is the likeliest home for a Genesis 6 singleton. The 1830 “hath I shewed” (1920: “have I shown”) preserves the King James spelling and, in “hath”, a grammatical form the later edition corrected — a small piece of §8 evidence that the sentence was composed in King James English rather than translated into it.
3:15.text: And the LORD said, I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth; both man, and beast, and the creeping thing, and the fowls of the air; for it repenteth me that I have made them.

provenance.route: Exodus 33:20 → KJV → Book of Mormon (thematic, not verbal)
provenance.other: “no man hath seen God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 1:18 and 1 John 4:12. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Ether 3:15 against Exodus 33:20, John 1:18 and 1 John 4:12: at every divergence it reports “neither — the BoM reads otherwise here”. There is no verbal case, and kjvSpecific is 'no' accordingly.
provenance.significance: The two King James statements of divine invisibility are Exodus 33:20, “there shall no man see me, and live”, and John 1:18, “No man hath seen God at any time”. Ether 3:15 puts the claim in God's own mouth in a chapter that is in the act of breaking it — and the chapter's answer is John 1:18's answer, that what is seen is the Son who declares the Father. Note the standing difficulty this verse creates for its own book, since Exodus 33:11 has the LORD speaking to Moses face to face and the Book of Mormon elsewhere has men see God; the sentence is best read as bounded by its context, no man has believed like this, and therefore none has seen like this.

3:15.whyNot: There is no shared wording and the mediation check finds none: the link is entirely a matter of doctrine and situation. A reader who requires verbal contact should decline it. It is recorded because a catalogue of the Bible in this chapter that said nothing about Exodus 33 would be hiding the passage every reader arrives with.
3:15.note: “And never hath I shewed myself unto man whom I have created.” The claim is the Old Testament's rule of divine invisibility asserted in the first person at the moment it is being suspended, and Exodus 33:20 is where the King James Bible states that rule. The catalogue files this as figural because the verbal test is negative and says so plainly rather than manufacturing a case; what carries it is that the chapter's own solution to Exodus 33's problem is the solution John 1:18 gives — the invisible God is seen in the Son, who is exactly who Ether 3:14 has just said is speaking.
3:15.text: And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.

provenance.other: “manifest in the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:16, where it stands in antithesis with “justified in the Spirit”. No Old Testament verse sets flesh and spirit in this particular opposition as modes of a divine appearing.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 3:16 is the King James Bible's compressed creed — God manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit — and Ether 3:16 is that couplet re-ordered into chronology: “even as I appear unto thee to be in the spirit, will I appear unto my people in the flesh.” The epistle's order is confessional, flesh first because the incarnation is what the confession is about; Ether's order is temporal, spirit first because the brother of Jared is standing on the earlier side of it. Recovering the epistle explains why the sentence has that shape: it is a creed being spoken from before the events it confesses.

3:16.note: “Even as I appear unto thee to be in the spirit, will I appear unto my people in the flesh.” The spirit/flesh antithesis as two modes of one divine appearing is 1 Timothy 3:16's, and “manifest in the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What is being borrowed is a structure rather than a string — the balanced pair, with the same subject and the same verb in both halves — which is why this is an allusion at high rather than a quotation. The chapter needs a way to say that the body now shown is the body later born, and it reaches for the one King James sentence that holds the two states together.
3:16.text: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

provenance.other: “the Word was made flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:14, and Ether 3:16 does not reproduce it — the contact is with the prologue's argument, not its famous clause, which is why the verbal scores here are modest. The prologue supplies the chapter with four separate points of contact: the light shining in darkness (1:4-5) at 3:14, the power to become sons to them that believe on his name (1:12) at 3:14, the invisible God declared by the Son (1:18) at 3:15, and the Word made flesh (1:14) here.
provenance.significance: Ether 3 is the Book of Mormon's prologue to John, and it is arranged the way John's is. The prologue moves from a pre-existent Word who is with God and is God, through light in darkness, through the power to become sons, to flesh; Ether 3:14-16 moves from one who was prepared from the foundation of the world and is both Father and Son, through light for all mankind, through becoming sons and daughters, to “I appear … in the flesh”. What John narrates in retrospect this chapter states as a promise, which is precisely the difference the availability question makes and precisely what the catalogue exists to record.

3:16.note: “And even as I appear unto thee to be in the spirit, will I appear unto my people in the flesh.” The verse says what John 1:14 says — the one who is with God takes flesh and is beheld — with the tense moved forward. The verbal contact is confined to “flesh” and the argument rests on the prologue's presence throughout 3:14-16: four of John 1's distinctive claims appear in three consecutive verses, in John's own order. Note the 1830's “which was prepared” and “they which shall believe” at 3:14, KJV relative pronouns that the 1920 edition modernised to “who”; the paragraph was composed in the prologue's English as well as its argument.
3:16.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.route: John 21:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon; possibly by way of 3 Nephi 11 (see alternative)
provenance.other: “shewed himself” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: John 21:1, John 21:14, Acts 1:3 and Acts 7:26. The first three are all resurrection appearances; the fourth is Moses showing himself to the quarrelling Hebrews. The 1830 spelling “shewed” is the KJV's; the 1920 edition prints “showed” at both occurrences in this verse, so the first edition shows the contact more plainly than the current text does (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.alternative: The proximate model may not be the Bible at all. Moroni's own sentence keys the appearance to another Book of Mormon passage — “even as he shewed himself unto the Nephites” — and the catalogue already carries 3 Nephi 11:14 → John 20:27 as a certain link, with 3 Nephi 11:15's witnesses going forward “one by one” as Ether 3:6's stones are touched one by one. So the shape here is a New Testament source reaching this verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage, and the mediation enum has no value for it: OT-via-earlier-BoM covers only an Old Testament source. Recorded as direct-NT with the route stated here rather than by inventing a sixth value; the honest description is John's phrase arriving via 3 Nephi 11, on Moroni's own cross-reference.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible's verb for a risen Christ making himself visible to witnesses is shew, and it belongs to a small closed set of post-resurrection scenes. Moroni applies it to an appearance that happens two thousand years before the resurrection and then, in the same sentence, licenses the application by pointing at the Nephite theophany — so the vocabulary of Easter is being used, deliberately and with a cross-reference, for a pre-incarnate visit.

3:17.note: “That Jesus shewed himself unto this man in the spirit, even after the manner and in the likeness of the same body, even as he shewed himself unto the Nephites.” The verb is the KJV's post-resurrection idiom, with four instances and three of them appearances of the risen Christ, and the 1830 keeps the King James spelling that the 1920 edition removed. Held at moderate because “shewed himself” is a short phrase and because the route is genuinely unsettled — Moroni's own comparison suggests the model is 3 Nephi 11 rather than John directly, which the mediation field cannot presently express.
3:17.text: After these things Jesus shewed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias; and on this wise shewed he himself.

provenance.other: The spelling settles the source. “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:19; the tabernacle passages spell it otherwise, and “within the vail” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Exodus 26:33, Leviticus 16:2, 16:12, 16:15 and Numbers 18:7. Ether 3:19-20 and Ether 12:19 all read “veil”.
provenance.significance: Within the vail is a cultic restriction in the Pentateuch: Leviticus 16:2 warns Aaron not to come there at all times “that he die not”, because that is where God appears. Hebrews 6:19 takes the same words and makes them a destination — hope as an anchor entering into that within the veil. Ether 3:19 says the brother of Jared “could not be kept from beholding within the veil”, which is Leviticus' prohibition overridden by Hebrews' promise, in Hebrews' spelling. The chapter's other veil, at 3:6, was Paul's Moses-veil lifted from the eyes; this one is the temple curtain passed through. The same English word carries both and the chapter uses each in its own source's sense.

3:19.note: “He could not be kept from beholding within the veil.” Two spellings of one word divide the King James evidence cleanly, and the Book of Mormon has the Epistle's: “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:19, against five instances of the tabernacle's “within the vail”. That is a small orthographic fact carrying a large argument, since the two readings mean opposite things — Leviticus forbids the approach and Hebrews promises it — and Ether 3:19 is a sentence about a man who cannot be kept out. The formula recurs at 3:20 and again at Ether 12:19 for the many whose faith was strong before Christ came, so it is the book's fixed term for this experience rather than a single flourish.
3:19.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

provenance.other: “things not seen” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 11:1 and 11:7 — and 11:7 is Noah, “warned of God of things not seen as yet”, preparing an ark to the saving of his house, which is what the Jaredite barges of Ether 2 are built to be. Ether 3:19 reproduces neither phrase, so kjvSpecific is 'no': the borrowing is of the definition, not of the words. Ether 12:6 restates Hebrews 11:1 almost as a definition — “faith is things which are hoped for and not seen” — so the epistle's opening verse is demonstrably in this book's hands, nine chapters later, in the same author's voice.
provenance.significance: Ether 3:19 is the negative of Hebrews 11:1 and the book knows it. If faith is the evidence of things not seen, then a man who sees has, by definition, exchanged it for something else — which is exactly the sentence: “he had faith no longer, for he knew”. Moroni then does the arithmetic explicitly at 12:19, where the strong-faithed “truly saw with their eyes the things which they had beheld with an eye of faith”. Paul's “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7) is the same equation with the same terms. What the chapter adds to both is the claim that the exchange can happen in this life and did.

3:19.note: “And he had faith no longer, for he knew, nothing doubting.” The doctrine is Hebrews 11:1's, taken as a definition and then run backwards: since faith is the evidence of things not seen, sight ends it. That the book is working from that verse and not merely from a general idea is shown at Ether 12:6, where Moroni states Hebrews 11:1 in his own words before building the whole faith chapter on it. Filed as figural because the contact is conceptual rather than verbal, and at high because the same author quotes the source in the same book.
3:19.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “nothing doubting” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:12. The near variants are Acts 10:20's “doubting nothing” and James 1:6's “nothing wavering”; the Book of Mormon has Acts 11:12's word order.
provenance.significance: The context of the singleton is Peter explaining to Jerusalem why he entered a Gentile house: the Spirit bade him go, nothing doubting, and the chapter that follows is the church's decision that the promise is not confined to Israel. Ether 3 is the Book of Mormon's demonstration of the same proposition at the far end of history — its recipient of the fullest revelation in the book is not merely a Gentile but a man from before the covenant existed. The phrase joins Matthew 8:10 at 3:9 in a small pattern: the chapter's borrowings keep coming from the New Testament's passages about faith found outside Israel.

3:19.note: “For he knew, nothing doubting.” Two words, and they occur together in exactly one KJV verse. The entry would not stand on rarity alone — the phrase is easy to arrive at, and Acts 10:20 has the same two words the other way round — but the source verse is Peter's account of going to Cornelius, which makes it the third borrowing in this chapter from a New Testament passage about faith outside the covenant people, after Matthew 8:10 at 3:9. Held at moderate; recorded because the pattern is worth being able to see.
3:19.text: And the Spirit bade me go with them, nothing doubting. Moreover these six brethren accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house:

provenance.other: “through the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:20 — the one verse in the King James Bible that identifies the veil with a body: “through the veil, that is to say, his flesh”. It shares the Epistle's “veil” spelling with Hebrews 6:19 and with Ether 3:19-20 and 12:19, against the Pentateuch's “vail” (see the note at 3:19).
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's densest piece of metalepsis and it is entirely unstated. Ether 3:20 says that the brother of Jared could not be kept from within the veil and therefore saw Jesus. Hebrews 10:20 says that the way within the veil is itself the flesh of Christ. Put the two together and the chapter's sequence becomes an argument rather than a series of marvels: the man passes the veil, and what he finds on the other side is the flesh — which is what the veil was. The one thing that made him fear he would die at 3:8, that the Lord had flesh and blood, is the very thing that let him through.

3:20.note: “He could not be kept from within the veil; therefore he saw Jesus, and he did minister unto him.” The verse has no long borrowing; what it has is Hebrews' technical vocabulary at 3:19 and Hebrews' conclusion here. Filed at moderate because the argument depends on the reader recovering Hebrews 10:20 rather than on shared wording, and because a reader who declines the recovery is left with a bare statement. But the pairing of the Epistle's spelling of the veil with the Epistle's doctrine of what lies behind it, in a chapter whose whole subject is a divine body, is more than the words alone would predict.
3:20.text: By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;

provenance.other: “tell the vision to no man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 17:9; Mark 9:9 carries the same command without the noun. “glorify thy name” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which John 12:28 is the one that means the passion.
provenance.significance: Both verses are the same scene from opposite ends. Matthew 17:9 is the descent from the Mount of Transfiguration: three men have seen Christ in glory on a mountain, and the first thing they are told is to tell the vision to no man until the resurrection. Ether 3:21 is the descent from Shelem: a man has seen Christ in glory on a mountain, and the first thing he is told is to shew it to no man until “the time cometh that I shall glorify my name in the flesh”. Even the terminus matches — Matthew's “until the Son of man be risen again from the dead” and Ether's glorification in the flesh are the same event under two descriptions, and John 12:28's “Father, glorify thy name” is the King James verse where that description is the passion's.

3:21.note: “Thou shalt not suffer these things which ye have seen and heard, to go forth unto the world, until the time cometh that I shall glorify my name in the flesh … and shew it to no man.” This is the messianic-secret command of Matthew 17:9, with its two parts intact and in order: silence about a mountain vision, bounded by a date that is the glorification of the one seen. The King James Bible issues that command once in those terms. The 1830's “shew” is the KJV spelling, modernised in 1920. Below quotation length, and the sequence and context scores are what carry it — a seal placed on a mountaintop vision until the flesh is glorified is not a general biblical motif but a single gospel scene.
3:21.text: And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, saying, Tell the vision to no man, until the Son of man be risen again from the dead.

provenance.other: “the words of a book that is sealed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:11. The catalogue already carries Isaiah 29:11 as a certain quotation at 2 Nephi 27:15 and 27:17 and as a certain allusion at 27:6, so the sealed-book passage is established in this corpus long before Ether.
provenance.significance: The mediation call is the finding. Ether 3:22's sentence has no verbal contact with Isaiah 29:11 at all — “a language that they cannot be read” is nobody's King James phrase — but it has close contact with 2 Nephi 27, which is itself Isaiah 29 with additions, and the additions are where the contact lies: sealing, the impossibility of reading, the promise of a later unsealing “in mine own due time”. So the Isaianic material reaches Ether through the Book of Mormon's own earlier expansion of it rather than through the KJV directly, which is exactly the case OT-via-earlier-BoM exists to record and, on this book's chronology, the first place in Ether where it can be shown.

3:22.note: “Ye shall write them and shall seal them up, that no one can interpret them: for ye shall write them in a language that they cannot be read.” The picture is Isaiah 29:11's — a sealed book handed to a reader who says he cannot read it — and the King James phrase for it occurs in exactly one verse. But the wording that actually stands behind Ether 3:22 is 2 Nephi 27's, where the same Isaiah passage has already been expanded with the sealing, the withholding and the due time that Ether 3:22-27 then reuses. Filed as OT-via-earlier-BoM on that ground: the source is Isaiah, the model is 2 Nephi.
3:22.text: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:

provenance.other: “I will give thee tables of stone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 24:12; “tables of stone” occurs in exactly thirteen, all of them Sinai or its recital.
provenance.significance: The chapter opened on the mountain with worked stone in a man's hands and closes with God promising to give him two more, which is the Sinai transaction in reverse — Moses brings stone up and receives writing, the brother of Jared brings stone up and receives light, and is then given two stones so that his writing can be read. The suppressed correspondence is the function: at Sinai the stone carries the text; here the stone is what makes the text legible. Exodus 24:12's promise ends “that thou mayest teach them”, and Ether 3:24 ends with the stones magnifying the writing “to the eyes of men”.

3:23.note: “And behold, these two stones will I give unto thee, and ye shall seal them up also, with the things which ye shall write.” The King James Bible has one verse in which God says he will give a man stone: “Come up to me into the mount, and be there: and I will give thee tables of stone.” Ether 3 has already put its man on the mount with stone in his hands (3:1) and has already asked for God's finger on it (3:4); this is the same scene's closing move with the number reduced from many to two and the purpose changed from inscription to interpretation. The machine stream offered Jeremiah 45:5 here on “will I give unto thee”, which is the wrong half of the sentence — see the exclusion register.
3:23.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Come up to me into the mount, and be there: and I will give thee tables of stone, and a law, and commandments which I have written; that thou mayest teach them.

provenance.other: “the LORD shewed him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 15:25 (a tree at Marah) and Deuteronomy 34:1. Only Deuteronomy 34:1 is a panorama, and it is the only place in the King James Bible where God shows a man everything from a mountain top. The 1830 spelling “shewed” is the KJV's and was modernised in 1920.
provenance.significance: The Moses frame that opened at 3:1 closes here, and it closes on the last page of the Pentateuch. Moses goes up to the top of Pisgah and the LORD shews him all the land, to its furthest boundary, and it is the last thing he sees. The brother of Jared, on the top of Shelem, is shewn “all the inhabitants of the earth which had been, and also all that would be … even unto the ends of the earth”. Deuteronomy's panorama is spatial and terminal — a country he will not enter, seen instead of possessed; Ether's is temporal and total, and it is given to a man who will cross the water Moses did not.

3:25.note: “The Lord shewed unto the brother of Jared all the inhabitants of the earth which had been, and also all that would be; and the Lord withheld them not from his sight, even unto the ends of the earth.” In the King James Bible God shows a man a complete view from a summit exactly once, at Deuteronomy 34:1, and the verb in the 1830 text is spelled as the KJV spells it. The clause about withholding takes the chapter back to Job 42:2 (see 3:4), where “no thought can be withholden from thee” is the other half of the verse Ether 3:4 borrowed — so this verse gathers the chapter's two governing sources, Moses on the mountain and Job at the moment his eye sees. The machine stream's Luke 4:5 is a better verbal match and a worse one in every other respect; see the exclusion register.
3:25.text: And Moses went up from the plains of Moab unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. And the LORD shewed him all the land of Gilead, unto Dan,

provenance.other: “shut up the words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 12:4. The catalogue already carries Daniel 12:4 as a link at 2 Nephi 27:22, and 2 Nephi 27:21 reads “I will bring them forth in mine own due time: for I will shew unto the children of men” — which is Ether 3:27's sentence almost word for word, and is not in Isaiah or Daniel.
provenance.significance: Two commands to seal a text until an appointed time, and the second is nearer the Book of Mormon's own earlier rewriting than to either biblical source. Daniel supplies the instruction and the terminus; 2 Nephi 27 supplies the actual English — “in mine own due time”, “unto the children of men” — and Ether 3:27 reproduces it. What the mediation field records is that the Bible is behind this verse at one remove, with the Book of Mormon's own prophetic idiom in between, and Ether 4:7 will complete the arc by naming the condition for the unsealing.

3:27.note: “Write these things and seal them up, and I will shew them in mine own due time unto the children of men.” The command to seal a revelation until a set time is Daniel 12:4's, whose “shut up the words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. But the sentence's actual words are 2 Nephi 27:21's — “I will bring them forth in mine own due time: for I will shew unto the children of men” — a clause that belongs to the Book of Mormon's expansion of Isaiah 29 and to no biblical verse at all. Filed at moderate and as OT-via-earlier-BoM: Daniel is the source, the earlier Nephite passage is the model, and the 1830's “shew” preserves the King James spelling in both.
3:27.text: But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.
